stem: A propagation report excludes ten failed cuttings because they were discarded before final scoring, without a documented exclusion rule. What is the problem?
choices: The denominator was changed after the outcome by removing known failures, which can inflate the reported rooting success.
The exclusion is acceptable if discarded cuttings were no longer present at the final observation point.
Only successful cuttings should remain in the final propagation metric because rooting rate is intended to describe viable output.
The denominator matters only when comparing batches of different starting size; here the numerator is sufficient.
rationale: If failed cuttings were part of the original batch and no predefined exclusion rule applies, removing them after the outcome changes the denominator in a way that makes performance look better. A valid rate needs a controlled denominator established before or independently of the observed success/failure outcome. Post hoc exclusions weaken comparability and can bias performance reporting.
